body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about wind (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students observe and describe things moved by the wind, adding a drawing for detail (SL.K.4, SL.K.5).
- Students sort what they saw into groups, count each group and say which has the most and the fewest (K.MD.B.3, K.CC.B.5).
- Science focus: wind is moving air; we know it is there because we feel it and see what it pushes, and a stronger wind pushes harder.

MATERIALS
- Paper pinwheels or streamers on sticks (one per student or pair)
- A hand fan or folded paper fans for gentle and strong wind
- Light and heavy objects to test: a feather, a tissue, a crayon, a block
- Clipboards with three tally rows (leaves, flags, other) for the wind walk
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read We Cannot See the Wind together. Students wave paper fans at their own faces: can you feel the air move? Can you see it? Check the weather chart: is today windy?
Day 2: Lesson activity: What Wind Can Do. Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking and draw something the wind pushes. Test fans on a feather and a block: which one moves?
Day 3: Wind Hunt. Take pinwheels or streamers outside. Students look for things the wind moves, then draw one and record themselves telling about it. If the day is calm, use fans in class and try again on a breezier day.
Day 4: Wind Walk Count. Read the class wind walk aloud while you show 5, 2 and 1 counters. Students count each group and compare. Make your own tally on a real wind walk if the weather allows.
Day 5: Assessment: Wind Check. Read the pinwheel story and each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw a windy day.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: let students blow on a pinwheel gently and then hard before answering which spins faster. Use counters lined up in rows for counting.
- Support: accept "it moves things" as a first answer to "what is wind", then model "wind is moving air" and have students echo it.
- Stretch: ask which objects the gentle wind could move and which only the strong wind could move, and why. Ask how many more leaves than flags we saw.
- Multilingual learners: teach gentle and strong with a small and a big fan motion. Use the frames with pictures (a leaf, a flag, a kite) beside each blank.
- Calm week? Wind changes from day to day. Keep the pinwheels by the window and return to the wind hunt on the first windy day.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning about wind. Wind is moving air: we cannot see it, but we can feel it and see what it moves. On a walk or from a window, play "wind detective" with your child: what is the wind moving right now? Is it a gentle wind or a strong wind? You can make a simple streamer from a strip of paper and a stick and watch it together.
title: Teacher guide: Wind on the Move
